title: Alpha Is Bollywood's First Female-Led Spy Film. The Trolls Are Terrified — and That's the Point.
excerpt: Alia Bhatt turns wolf in the YRF Spy Universe's boldest swing yet. Then the internet manufactured a feud with Sharvari out of thin air.
body:
The teaser opens in the dark. A girl, barely more than a shadow, being told the oldest lesson in the world: there are predators, and there is prey, and you do not get to choose which one you are — until you do. Then Alia Bhatt looks up, something cold and final settling into her face, and decides to be the wolf. By the time The First Kill faded to black on June 10, the internet had already picked its side. Several sides, actually. All of them loud.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=0d4nirTymmg

This is Alpha, and it is doing the thing only the YRF Spy Universe knows how to do: arriving as an event before it has shown you almost anything at all.

Let's be clear about what makes this one different. Pathaan, War, the Tiger films — for nearly a decade, the most expensive, most testosterone-soaked franchise in Hindi cinema has been a boys' club where women were the romance, the rescue, or the reveal. Alpha is the first film in that universe fronted entirely by women. Alia Bhatt and Sharvari are the leads. Not the love interests. The leads. Produced by Aditya Chopra, directed by Shiv Rawail, with Bobby Deol as the mentor who forges Bhatt's assassin and Anil Kapoor circling the edges, it lands worldwide on July 3 — in a head-to-head clash with Huma Qureshi's Baby Do Die Do, because two desi female-assassin films opening the same day is exactly the kind of cinematic chaos 2026 deserves.

And Bhatt, in the teaser, is magnetic. Lean, feral, stripped of every soft edge the industry has ever asked her to perform. The footage — titled The First Kill — is built entirely around her dynamic with Bobby Deol, a father-daughter, master-protégé equation that crackles. Deol, enjoying the best late-career run of his life, leans into the menace.

**"Wishing you all the joy in the world & more." — Alia Bhatt

Star."**

"Amazing that we are making an action film in India like Alpha featuring two girls!" — Bobby Deol

!Spy Universe — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

He's not wrong to sound a little amazed. This shouldn't be a novelty in 2026. It still is.

But here's where the story turns from a trailer into a referendum. Within hours of the teaser dropping, a section of the internet wasn't talking about the action, the scale, or Bhatt's transformation. It was asking one question, over and over, in bad faith: where is Sharvari? The teaser featured Bhatt and Deol; Sharvari wasn't in it. From that single editorial choice, the trolls built an entire conspiracy — that Bhatt, threatened by a younger talent, had personally engineered her co-star out of the frame.

It's nonsense, and the makers said as much: the teaser was titled The First Kill for a reason. It exists to introduce the mentor-protégé spine of the film. A Sharvari-led teaser is coming. But the manufactured outrage exposed something real and unflattering about how a certain corner of the audience operates — because the same people performing concern for Sharvari had, days earlier, completely ignored her actual new release. Her Imtiaz Ali film Main Vaapas Aaunga, in which she stars opposite Vedang Raina and Diljit Dosanjh, opened June 12 to warm reviews and a cold box office. The love for Sharvari, it turns out, was only ever a stick to beat Alia with.

Bhatt, for her part, answered the noise the way she usually does — by ignoring it entirely. On June 14, Sharvari's birthday, she posted a never-before-seen clip of her co-star playing the piano.

"Happy birthday star. Wishing you all the joy in the world & more." — Alia Bhatt

Star. Not rival. The subtext wrote itself.

For the diaspora, this is a theatrical release, full stop — July 3 in cinemas across the US, UK, Canada, and the Gulf, the kind of weekend where NRI multiplexes in Edison, Wembley, and Brampton will be packed with families turning a Bollywood action film into an outing. Three songs — Haniya Ve, Massacre, and Champagne — have already cleared the censors, which tells you the soundtrack is built for both the dance floor and the trailer cuts. Expect the full Sharvari teaser, a music drop, and a final trailer before release.

Here's the take: the discourse around Alpha — the trolling, the conspiracy theories, the think-pieces — might be the best thing to happen to Hindi cinema all year. Not because it's pleasant, but because nobody manufactures outrage over a film they've already decided to ignore. They're scared of it. A two-woman action tentpole, backed without compromise by the biggest studio in the country, has rattled people badly enough to lie about it. That's not a red flag. That's a film that matters arriving exactly on time.
